Pro-orthology refers to, in this case, after-speciation gene duplication in the non-human species (aka 1:many orthology). CD59 antigen has a core architecture consisting of one UPAR/Ly-6 domain (Pfam:PF00021), a small domain of about 70 amino acids and containing 5 conserved disulfide bonds. It is both N- and O-glycosylated and is a GPI-anchored protein that releases soluble forms in some tissues."

### Cerebral edema `http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181`

#### Added
- Class: [Cerebral edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181) 

- [Cerebral edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181) [comment](http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#comment) "Cerebral edema refers to swelling within brain tissue due to the accumulation of fluid, and can occur as in response to almost any insulting agent. Edema canbe observed in and around regions of dead or dying brain, around metastases and abscesses, after traumatic injury, following hypoxic ischemic injury, and around primary brain tumors. There are at least five different types of edema: vasogenic, cytotoxic, hydrostatic, interstitial, and hypoosmotic. Three effects of edema are visible on imaging: (i) loss of gray-white matter differentiation; (ii) swelling of sulci (shrinking of gyri); and (iii) mass effects. On CT scanning, extensive low density may represent vasogenic edema. As the brain swells, not only do the sulci decrease, but all of the CSF spaces of the hemispheres (including the ventricles) decrease as well. Magnetic resonance tomography may show abnormalities of diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and Fluid attenuation inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences. Phenotype terms involving cerebral edema thus reflect inference about the underlying processes responsible for these abnormalities on brain imaging." 

- [Cerebral edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181) [label](http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#label) "Cerebral edema" 

- [Cerebral edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181) EquivalentTo [has part](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_0000051) some 
([edematous](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/PATO_0001450) and ([characteristic of part of](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/RO_0002314) some [telencephalon](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/UBERON_0001893)) and ([has modifier](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/RO_0002573) some [abnormal](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/PATO_0000460))) 

- [Cerebral edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181) SubClassOf [Edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0000969) 

- [Cerebral edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181) SubClassOf [Abnormal cerebral morphology](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002060) 

- [Cerebral edema](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0002181) SubClassOf [has part](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_0000051) some

### Coarctation of aorta `http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0001680`

#### Added
- Class: [Coarctation of aorta](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0001680) 

- [Coarctation of aorta](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0001680) [comment](http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#comment) "Coarctation refers to a narrowing of the lumen of a vessel producing an obstruction to flow. Coarctation can occur in any region of the aorta. Coarctation of the aorta is often a discrete obstruction commonly located in the descending thoracic aorta. More specifically, it is usually located in the juxtaductal position immediately distal to the left-subclavian artery in a left-sided arch. The hallmark clinical finding in coarctation of the aorta is hypertension proximal to the lesion, with diminished blood pressure distal to the obstruction. Consequently, clinical diagnosis can be made by the presence of diminished lower extremity pulses, differences in timing between upper extremity central pulses (often brachial) and lower extremity central pulses (often femoral), or the presence of a supine arm-leg blood pressure gradient." 

- [Coarctation of aorta](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0001680) [label](http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#label) "Coarctation of aorta"

([constricted](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/PATO_0001847) and ([characteristic of](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/RO_0000052) some [aorta](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/UBERON_0000947)) and ([has modifier](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/RO_0002573) some [abnormal](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/PATO_0000460))) 

- [Coarctation of aorta](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0001680) SubClassOf [Abnormal aortic morphology](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0001679) 

- [Coarctation of aorta](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0001680) SubClassOf [has part](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_0000051) some

### Tricuspid stenosis `http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0010446`

#### Added
- Class: [Tricuspid stenosis](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0010446) 

- [Tricuspid stenosis](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP_0010446) [comment](http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#comment) "Tricuspid stenosis results in characteristic changes in the jugular venous pulse in the form of leisurely V to Y descent and prominent a-waves. The liver is enlarged with a firm edge and is pulsatile in presystole. This is best appreciated with one hand on the liver edge and one on the precordium. Auscultation reveals a low- to medium-pitched diastolic rumble with inspiratory accentuation. This is usually localized to the lower sternal border."
